You are helping somebody think through what an event they expect would set off,
step by step, until the story reaches something they could actually trade.

You do this one step at a time. Each time we ask, we show you the map as it
stands and point at one claim on it, and you answer with a single next piece.
Somebody watches the map grow as your answers arrive, so a small, well-argued
piece beats a large, vague one.

What a claim is.
A claim is something that will be plainly true or false by a date, settled by a
named source. "Tensions ease" is not a claim, because two honest people will
never agree on whether it happened. "At least fourteen consecutive days of
unrestricted commercial transit through the Strait of Hormuz, counted by Lloyd's
List, by the first of November" is a claim, because they will. Every claim you
write carries the test, the name of whoever applies it, and the day by which the
answer is known.

Start from the outside, then come inside. Before you say how likely this claim
is, ask what set of past cases it belongs to, how many of them came out true, and
out of how many. Say what that set was, precisely enough that somebody else could
count it again. Then say how likely this particular claim is, with the honest
range around it — wide when you are reaching, narrow when you are on familiar
ground. The range is how sure you are of your own number. Where there is no
honest set of past cases, leave it out; absent is better than invented.

What an arrow is.
An arrow is a claim about a mechanism: this happening moves the odds of that.
It says which way and how hard it pushes, how many whole days it takes to arrive,
and what it does over time — a spike that fades, a switch that stays on, or a
climb that builds and then holds. It says whether the push survives its cause
going away: a toppled domino stays down, while an apple only stays up while the
desk is under it. And it says, in one to three sentences, why the mechanism is
real. An arrow with a number and no reason is worth nothing to the person reading
it.

Where the backing comes from.
Use the search tool when the ground is checkable and you are not certain of it,
and cite only addresses the search returned to you in this same call. If you did
not search, or nothing useful came back, cite nothing and say what you know in
the reason instead. An empty list of citations is an honest answer we can show.
An address you are recalling rather than reading is not backing, and we will not
treat it as backing.

How a story ends.
A chain ends either at something somebody could put money on — a contract at a
named venue with the side you would take, or an instrument with a direction and
how far you expect its price to move — or at a plain statement that there is
nothing to trade here, and why. Both are good endings. An ending that trails off
into prose is not.

What an answer is.
Exactly one of three things:
  a new claim, together with the one arrow that reaches it from a claim already
  on the map;
  an arrow between two claims that are both already on the map;
  or a note that this part of the story is finished, with one sentence saying
  why.

You never name a new claim with anything but its words. The short names in the
map we show you are ours; point at one when you name a cause, and never invent
another.

Status: three pull requests are open (#29, #30, #31). Both code branches are in fix rounds after my review. Spend is still $0.

**The pipeline (M).**
- **Review and fix round.** M split the 1,622-line `expand.py` into one-way modules, and `expand.py` itself is now 363 lines. The Verify door now uses the same best-backed-route rule as the change list. The vendor library is named in one module only, and a test enforces that.
- **The first live recording was refused.** Every call failed with `For 'anyOf', '$defs' is not supported`, because a union of three shapes can't sit at the top of a structured-output schema. A refused call costs nothing, so nothing was recorded and nothing was spent. I deleted the error recordings.
- **An open question closed wrongly.** The `proposals.md` question about this had been closed as "yes" because the client library accepted the union. M is wrapping it in a one-field envelope on the wire only, and is checking every schema we send against the documented limits before I try again. M is also correcting the chapter. I added this as lesson 15 in the handoff.

**The join (J).** It works, and the engine's numbers match what the engine tells me directly. From its screenshots I sent back four things:
- tiles collide on the branch view
- a false sentence on the base map
- "no engine yet" shown on a branch the engine refused
- a stale "No numbers yet." in the announcement line

**The path product.** No server route carries it today, and the browser must not multiply numbers. It stays an honest absence in the join. The engine gains it in 04b, and the growing-canvas pull request wires it.

Running now: J (fix round), M (schema fix) and F (the flaky property test on the fix branch). Once M finishes I re-record, which is about five calls and under a dollar. I'll report the measured cost before anything larger runs.

<result>Fixed and committed. Nothing else is blocking a recording that I can find by reading.

## What changed

**The envelope.** `client.py` gains `OneProposal` — a frozen model with a single `proposal: Proposal` field. `_ask` sends that instead of the bare union; `what_it_said` takes it off before building `Said`. It exists for the wire and nothing else: no field of any proposal is renamed, `Proposal` is still the discriminated union of three shapes, and `expand` receives a plain `Proposal` exactly as before. `StartingClaim` is already an object at the top (`type: object`, `$defs` alongside) and is sent unwrapped.

**`wire_schema(shape)`** returns the exact description the library will send — the shape's own JSON schema after the library's tidying pass. It uses one private path into the SDK (`anthropic.lib._parse._transform.transform_schema`), in the one module allowed to know vendor internals, never to build a request, with a comment saying that if it moves the import fails loudly at start-up.

**`test_wire_schema.py`** (14 tests, both shapes) pins what the service demands. **`prompt_hash` now covers the shapes as they go out** rather than as they are written, since the tidied description is what the model is actually asked for: `93f8598…`. Nothing is recorded, so nothing is stale.

**`proposals.md` open question 2** rewritten in my worktree: answered *no*, with the service's sentence quoted, the envelope described as wire-only, and the note that the library and the service disagreed — which is why reading the library was not enough.

## The risks I found by reading

Measured: `OneProposal` is 15.9 KB, 10 named shapes, deepest nesting 9, largest object 10 properties; `StartingClaim` 5.1 KB.

**Clean, and now pinned by tests.** No unsupported keyword survives — the library strips every numeric and string constraint (`minimum`, `maximum`, `exclusiveMinimum`, `minLength`, …), so none reaches the wire. Every one of the 11 objects carries `additionalProperties: false`. The only string format is `date`, which is supported. No recursion. `tuple[X, ...]` is homogeneous so it emits a plain array — no `prefixItems`; a fixed-length tuple would, and the test now forbids one. Every `$ref` resolves. Multi-valued `Literal`s survive as real `enum`s (`mode`, `shape`, `claim_kind`, `side`, `direction`), so those *are* constrained by the service.

**Fixed.** *A discriminator is a hint, not a constraint, and on a payoff it is optional too.* The library moves a single-valued `const` into the description (`{"type":"string", "description":"… {const: claim}"}`) even though the bundle lists `const` as supported — so the model reads `kind` from prose. Worse, `ContractPayoff.kind` and `PricePayoff.kind` carry defaults in `domain/`, so they are **absent from `required`**: a model can legitimately omit the one field that tells the two payoff shapes apart, and pydantic then has nothing to route on. I could not fix the defaults (they are `domain/proposition.py`, not mine), so I spent the risk where it is cheapest and inside my own files: `ClaimProposal.payoff`'s description now names `kind` and both its values. **Worth a look from whoever owns `domain/proposition.py`** — giving those two fields no default would remove the hazard outright.

**Unsettled by the skill, left as they are, with the one-line fix named.**
- *Optional properties are absent from `required`.* The bundle requires only `additionalProperties: false` per object and nowhere says every property must be required; its tool guidance explicitly endorses optional parameters. Our optional fields mean what they say — an absent base rate is absent, not `null`. If the service objects, the fix is to make every field required and `| None`, which changes no meaning because each already accepts null.
- *Nested `anyOf`.* `payoff` is `anyOf[ anyOf[Contract, Price], null ]`. `anyOf` is supported and nothing says it may not nest; if it turns out it may not, flattening to `anyOf[Contract, Price, null]` is the fix.
- *No documented limit* on schema size, property count or nesting depth. Ours are small; the first successful call settles it.

**Already the designed path.** Because numeric constraints never reach the service, a likelihood outside 0–1 or a base rate with `n = 0` comes back as an answer we could not read — a refusal with a plain sentence, and G4's silent retry asks again. That is what `Ranged`'s own validator is for and it is documented there.

- **Relax the rule.** A recording shows every refusal that happened, and says plainly when there were none.
- **Grow larger maps.** Loops and bad proposals arise naturally in bigger maps.

## What changed

**A paid run is never discarded.** `run_one` now returns everything a run produced, and three separate things happen to it in a fixed order:

1. **The receipt is printed**, whatever the verdict — model, calls, searches, tokens fresh and read back from the cache, tokens out, dollars, seconds, **what share of the writing was thinking**, the quickest and slowest call, the stop reason with its plain sentence, and what it built.
2. **Everything is written to `backend/.runs/<example>-<timestamp>.json`** — always, before anybody asks whether it was good enough. It carries the transcript with the seconds and thinking tokens behind every call, the receipt, the `done` event, the prompt's fingerprint, the finished map, **and the events themselves**, so a run nobody can afford to repeat can still be read or salvaged. It also carries `became_a_recording` and the faults, so the file says why. The folder is git-ignored, and the terminal prints the path.
3. **Only then** do the checks decide whether it is *also* written to `backend/recordings/`. Those rules are untouched: one writer, nobody edits, re-run rather than repair.

**Nine silent minutes are now legible.** Each proposal prints as it lands:

```

```

with the running dollars and tokens every four calls.

**`make run-demo ONLY=… CAP=…`** is the same run meant as a measurement — one code path, one `--measure-only` flag — which keeps everything and writes no recording. `make record-demo` is unchanged in intent.

**Six tests** in `tests/unit/engine/test_record.py` against fake answers, including the exact case you hit: a run with no refusal writes no recording, **is still kept in full** (receipt with calls, done event, graph, prompt hash, per-line seconds and thinking tokens, the events), and prints its cost.

**Two real bugs found on the way.** The header's `base_id` was a freshly minted identifier rather than the identifier of the map the run actually built — a recording written before this fix would have described a map nothing could find. And the growth events were being collected into a list that was then discarded, so the recorder would have written a file holding only `generation_started`, `receipt` and `done`. Both are covered by the new tests. The outcome-to-event step also moved from the route into `events.py`, so an engine module no longer has to import a route to reach it.

```
make run-demo ONLY=hormuz CAP=15
```

It keeps everything under `backend/.runs/` and writes no recording, whatever the run does. If you want the same run to *also* become a recording when it earns one:

```
make record-demo ONLY=hormuz CAP=15

I now have what I need to bring you the batch of questions. First, the facts.

**The measured run (Hormuz, live, default settings).**
- 10 calls, 9 searches, **$1.32**.
- **10 min 54 s**, and 61% of everything the model wrote was thinking.
- It built 10 claims and 9 arrows. None were refused. It stopped at the width cap.
- The map is good. Hormuz leads to Brent, to VLCC rates (short Frontline), and to Qatari LNG. LNG leads to TTF, JKM and EU storage at 80%. Storage leads to Q1-2027 TTF, German power and a calendar spread.
- Every ending names a real instrument and a real judge: ICE, CME, Baltic Exchange, AGSI+.
- 8 of the 9 arrows are `documented`, with sources the search actually returned.
- The pace is about one tile a minute, and it is sequential by nature. Each call has to see the map as it stands, so "three at once" only helps when three different claims are open.

**What I'm fixing without asking.** Each of these is a defect or follows from something you already decided.

content.text:
Three answers are in: recordings show what actually happened, anything below .01 prints `<.01`, and the tile ceiling stays at 320 with the chapter corrected. Here is the base rate explained plainly.

**What a base rate is for.** Take a claim on the map: *"Europe ends the injection season with gas storage at least 80% full."* The model gives two things about it.

- **The likelihood**, `.30 (.12–.52)`. This is its judgment about this particular situation.
- **The base rate**, "12 of 15". It answers a different question: in past situations like this one, how often did it come out true? Here the claim is that in 15 past gas-supply scares, storage still reached 80% in 12 of them.

It exists because forecasters do better when they start from how often this kind of thing usually happens and only then adjust for the case in front of them. Your PRD asks for this: every number should be one click from "how often such things have happened before". On screen the base rate sits in the Inspector next to the likelihood, so a reader can see whether `.30` is a bold call against a usual 80% or just the ordinary rate.

**The problem.** The model gets one web search per step, and it always spends it on why the arrow is real (the mechanism). So "12 of 15" was never looked up. It is the model's memory, stated with the precision of a count. Nobody can click through and check which 15 episodes it means.

A reader cannot tell a counted number from a remembered one. That is the "number nobody computed" state you veto.

**The three choices.**

1. **Let it look the count up, and show only what it found.** The model gets a second search, reserved for the reference class. A base rate appears only when it cites a page that search returned. Otherwise the slot says honestly that there is none. This is the same rule you already chose for an arrow's sources.
   - Cost is about a cent per step, plus an estimated 15–30 seconds (I would measure it).
   - Most honest, keeps the feature alive, and slows a live run down.
2. **Same honesty rule, no extra search.** A base rate appears only if it is sourced, and with one search it almost never will be.
   - On this run all 8 would have disappeared.
   - Fast and simple, but the "how often before?" slot would nearly always be empty.
3. **Keep showing them, with a label.** "12 of 15" stays on screen with the words *recalled by the model — not counted from a source*.
   - Nothing slows down and nothing is lost.
   - A precise-looking count that nobody can check still sits next to your real numbers.

I recommend option 1. It treats a base rate exactly as you already treat an arrow's evidence, so there is one rule rather than two.

Total spend is about $5 of the $500 ceiling. I just checked the pull requests, the checks and the worktrees on disk, so this is the repository's state, not my memory of it.

## Progress against the whole prototype

| Stack | State |

| 01 skeleton, 02 schema, 03 engine + canvas | Merged. |
| **04 generation** | **In progress.** Details below. |

| **#30** → `main` | Five generation chapters, record 0015 (no ensemble), and dated amendments to records 0003, 0006, 0009 and 0012. |
| **#32** → #30 | The model pipeline: one proposal per call, validated by our own rules, tested on real recorded answers with no key. |

## Stack 04: built, not yet a pull request

| Piece | State |
|---|---|
| **The stream, replay, readiness, the recordings CI job, the nginx fix** (M) | Working and verified. |
| **The prompt round** (M) | In progress: Sonnet 5 as a setting, base-rate research, standalone claim wording, the junk-hypothesis fix, "Add a claim", three replay bugs. Your round-two decisions all change what we send the model, so they go in together and I re-record once. |
| **The growing canvas** (G) | Built, in a fix round. I found a blocking defect in its pictures: on a growing map, a new tile landed on top of an existing one. G is now testing against the real 10-claim run. |

## Stack 04: not started

- Evals and the scorecard.
- The provenance-derived spread on arrow strengths.
- The engine carrying the path's multiplied-out likelihood (INV-8).
- The final `ARCHITECTURE.md` and PRD sweep.
- The four final recordings.

## What the live runs taught us

- **The pipeline works.** A live Hormuz run on Opus 5 built a rich 10-claim map: Brent, tanker rates, Qatari LNG leading to European and Asian gas, EU storage, German power, and a calendar spread. It took 10 calls, cost **$1.32** and ran **11 minutes**. 8 of 9 arrows were backed by sources the search actually returned.
- **Pace is the main product risk.** A live run adds about one tile a minute, and it is sequential by design. 61% of what the model writes is thinking. Replay covers a reviewer with no key, but a live 30-claim map would take half an hour. Sonnet 5 and a lower thinking effort are the first things to try, and I will measure both.
- **The model was never refused** across 26 proposals. That is why you relaxed the recording rule.
- **Defects only real runs could find:**
  - The API refuses a schema that the client library accepts.
  - The first recorder discarded a paid run's measurements. I booked that run at $3.
  - The recordings carried your organisation and rate-limit headers. They are now stripped.
  - A minted seed was too large for a browser to hold exactly.

## Your decisions so far

All are recorded in the decisions note under `plans/notes/` and folded into the plan.

**Round one**
- No ensemble: the model's stated range ships, labelled as stated.
- The direction of a move is read with the same weights as the number.
- Up to three silent retries after a refusal. You chose this over my recommendation.
- A $500 ceiling for the stack, with a $15 hard stop per run in code.

**Round two**
- Base rates are researched: up to 25 searches over up to 5 rounds per claim, and shown only when sourced.
- Prototype on Sonnet 5.
- A recording shows what actually happened; no refusal is forced.
- A likelihood below `.01` prints `<.01`.
- The tile height ceiling is 320.

## What happens next, in order

1. M finishes the prompt round. I re-record the cassettes and run Hormuz on Sonnet 5 at default effort and at `medium`. I bring you cost, pace and map quality beside the Opus run. I will watch your per-claim research budget closely, because it is the biggest unknown for both cost and pace.
2. G's collision fix is verified on the real map. Then I rebase both stacks so they stay linear.
3. The stream pull request opens. The growing canvas opens after it, held until the stream is on `main`.
4. One last agent does the evals, the arrow-strength spread, the path likelihood and the documentation sweep. Then come the four final recordings.
5. **Milestone M4:** you look at a live generation and a replayed one.

## What needs you

Nothing is blocking. Two things would help when you have time:

- **Look at #33.** It is the first time the real engine's numbers are on the canvas, and it is where a template-looking interface would show up.
- **Tell me whether you want #29, #31 and #33 merged now.** They are complete and independent of the model work. Merging them would shrink the pile and let you see computed numbers on `main`.

Can you explain to me in more detail what these entail in simple terms?

Stack 04: not started

- Evals and the scorecard.
- The provenance-derived spread on arrow strengths.
- The engine carrying the path's multiplied-out likelihood (INV-8).
- The final ARCHITECTURE.md and PRD sweep.
- The four final recordings.

These are the five pieces of stack 04 that haven't been started. Here is what each one is, why it's there, and what it costs.

## 1. Evals and the scorecard

**What it is.** A command, `make eval`, that runs the four example hypotheses from the assignment through the real model and grades the resulting maps. It checks only structure and never wording:
- Are there any loops?
- Does every map end in something you could trade, or in a plain "nothing to trade here"?
- Does every arrow give a reason?
- Does every `documented` arrow have a source?
- Does every claim say how it will be checked?
- Does the Verify door return a graded path or an honest "no path"?
- One of the four cases is deliberately unreachable, to prove the engine never invents a bridge.

The output is a **scorecard**, a table with one row per example. It shows claims, endings, refusals, base rates kept and dropped, searches, thinking tokens, seconds per call and dollars.

**Why it exists.** Today, when I change the prompt, the only way to know whether it helped is to read a map and form an opinion. The scorecard turns "did that prompt change help?" into a comparison of two rows. It is also the baseline that your earlier decisions point at. The ensemble (record 0015) and the critique pass (FR-9) are both deferred until there is a scorecard to measure them against.

**Cost.** It calls the model, so only I run it, under the $15 stop. It is not part of the build, because continuous integration never gets a key.

## 2. The provenance-derived spread on arrow strengths

**What it is.** The engine computes every likelihood 2,000 times, on 2,000 slightly different versions of the map, to get a range like `.35 (.22–.50)`. Today only each claim's starting number varies between versions. Every arrow's strength is treated as exactly known.

This piece makes arrow strengths vary too. How much each one varies is derived from how well-backed the arrow is:

| The arrow is… | Its strength wobbles… |
|---|---|
| `documented` (cites a source) | a little (0.15) |
| `argued` (a rationale, no source) | more (0.40) |
| `asserted` (neither) | a lot (0.60) |

You settled this in record 0014. "How well-backed is this arrow?" becomes "how wide is the range downstream?" without asking the model for any extra numbers.

**Why it was deferred to here.** On the hand-written Hormuz example, almost every arrow has the same backing. The spread would have widened everything equally and taught nothing. Generated maps genuinely mix `documented` and `argued` arrows, so now it means something. On the live run, 8 arrows were documented and 1 was argued. After this change, a map built on sourced mechanisms shows visibly tighter ranges than one built on argument alone.

**The catch.** It changes every computed number. Every number quoted in the spec chapters goes stale at once, so the sweep of those chapters has to travel in the same pull request. That was a hard-won lesson from stack 03.

## 3. The engine carrying the path's multiplied-out likelihood (INV-8)

**What it is.** A causal chain reads persuasively: strait opens, then insurance gets cheaper, then Brent falls. But if each step is 60% likely, the whole chain is about 22%, and stories hide that. Your invariant INV-8 says every path must show its multiplied-out likelihood beside the story, so a convincing narrative can't pass for a likely one.

**Where it stands.** The Inspector's path bar has a slot for this number. When J joined the canvas to the engine, it found that no server route carries the number. Your rule is that the browser never does arithmetic, since a second place that computes numbers is a second engine that will drift. So the slot honestly says "not worked out".

**The work.** It is small. The engine already has the one path-choosing rule, the best-backed route, which M made public for the Verify door. This piece multiplies along that route and puts the result on the world the engine returns. The growing-canvas pull request then shows it.

## 4. The final `ARCHITECTURE.md` and PRD sweep

**What it is.** Your working agreement says `ARCHITECTURE.md` is living: every section is marked *built* or *planned*, and it must match reality. Stack 04 makes a lot of "planned" things real:
- the event stream
- the model boundary
- replay mode
- the recorded-response test layer
- a sixth CI job
- new folders

This pass updates those sections and corrects the test counts. The document says 137 server tests. There are now over 400. It also marks stack 04 done in the PRD's roadmap table and closes the PRD's answered open questions.

**Why it comes last.** It describes both halves, browser and server, so it can only be written truthfully once both are finished. It is documentation only. For a reviewer judging "rigorously documented decisions", this is the page that has to be true.

## 5. The four final recordings

**What it is.** A reviewer who clones the repo with no API key still gets the whole experience. The four example cards on the launchpad play back real recorded generations through the same route, the same stream and the same canvas as a live run. Record 0012 made this a requirement. The four are Hormuz, the midterms, export restrictions on AI models, and photonic chips. For each, the recording also stores one scripted "…but this also happens" intervention.

**Why none exist yet.** A recording is only valid for the exact prompt that produced it. CI fails if a recording's prompt fingerprint doesn't match the current prompt. Recording before the prompt settles means paying to record twice. Your round-two decisions all change the prompt: researched base rates, Sonnet 5, and standalone claim wording. That is why M's prompt round comes first.

**Cost.** Four full generations. On Opus the measured run was $1.32 and 11 minutes for a 10-claim map. Sonnet 5 should be cheaper per token. Your per-claim research budget of up to 25 searches will add to it. I will measure one run first and tell you the real figure before recording all four. Only I run these, with the $15 per-run stop in place.

## How they fit together

Most of this is one last agent's work. Items 1 to 4 go in a single final pull request on the server side, since items 2 and 3 both touch the engine's arithmetic and item 4 documents the result. Item 5 is mine to run and comes at the very end, because the recordings must be made against the final prompt and the final engine. The order is:

1. the prompt round
2. measurement runs
3. that last pull request
4. the four recordings
5. you look at a live map and a replayed one

input.message:
Coordinator to J — Kent has asked me to merge stack 04a once its work is done, and an independent read-only reviewer went over #29/#31/#33 first. It found four defects that must be fixed before the merge, all in your branch, plus smaller ones. Same worktree and branch (`feat/04a-join`, tip `f1ef102`); commit on top in small commits, do not rewrite history (G is forked off you), do not push. For each must-fix: write the failing test FIRST, watch it fail, then fix.

**Must fix before merge**
1. **The arrow-number cache is keyed on a branch identity that does not change when the branch changes.** `App.tsx` `wireKey` is `${openId}:${seed}:${linkId}`; `appendEdit` returns a new branch with the same `id`. Start a branch → select `H→B` (conditional cached) → press **This happened** on C: the world and diff are re-asked but the OLD conditional is re-attached and never re-fetched — a number for a branch that no longer exists, with nothing saying so. `App.test.tsx` tests the cache hit, not the invalidation. A branch is append-only, so its edit count (or the wire branch's `interventions.length`) in the key is sufficient and honest — but check: can an edit ever be removed or replaced? If so use something that changes then too.
2. **A branch's conditional is drawn on the map "as it was written", and is fetched for the branch while that map is showing.** `wireKey` ignores `showing`; `paintings.before.links` share ids with the branch's. Open a branch, select an arrow, press Space: the header says *as it was written* and the wire still carries the branch's number; selecting an arrow WHILE showing "before" asks `readConditional` for the branch and paints it on the unedited map. A number on screen belongs to a map the reader is not looking at — a veto. Key and fetch by the map actually showing.
3. **The tile's "no change" badge gives a false reason in the reweighting case.** `graph/diff/branchWorld.ts` ~150–162 says "its likelihood did not move by enough to report". A claim is `unchanged` when the move is under the floor OR the same-direction share is under 90%. Observing C moves H by `.0090` — nearly twice the floor — with a share of exactly 0, and the tile asserts the one thing that is not true of it. The Inspector already has the right sentence for each case; this is one rule written in two places with one copy wrong. One source for the reason, chosen by what the engine's row says (under the floor / versions did not agree / moved only by reweighting). Extend the end-to-end test to read the tile's badge reason in that case.
4. **The Inspector's decomposition lists feedback arrows as pushes.** `Inspector.tsx` ~214 filters `world.links` by target with no `reflexive` test. K1 (binding): anything that asks "what can move" reads the map with feedback arrows set aside. Selecting R shows `B pushes …` — a push that contributed nothing to the number two lines below. The outline already says "Fed back into by"; use the same words, listed apart from the pushes, and say it contributed nothing to this number yet.

**Should fix now, while you are there**
5. `roomFor` (`App.tsx` ~355–366) adds and subtracts already-clamped heights, so it can hand the layout a tile taller than 320 (worked: 320 + 280 − 248 = 352) — reachable on generated maps. Compute the natural height once and clamp once; make `layout.test.ts` call `roomFor` rather than typing heights in.
6. An observation of FALSE would read **Happened** (`apiSource.ts` ~125–132, ~171–183): the `do` path passes the value, the `observe` path does not. Not reachable from today's buttons, reachable from a stored branch. Read `spec/vocabulary.md` for the word an observed-false claim takes; if there is none, tell me and use the plainest true words meanwhile.
7. A conditional that fails once is cached as an absence and never retried, and it says "no engine yet" when the engine was reached and failed (`App.tsx` ~552–565). Do not cache a failure; use the absence kind that is true.
8. `engineState()` mints a new object every render, so the whole branch world is rebuilt on every keystroke — memoise on the answer.
12. `whereItsDaySits` uses an exact `indexOf` where the engine clamps to `[0, days]` — mirror the engine's clamp so a supposed claim never prints the stored `1.0` as `>.99`.
Nits: 13 (`layoutRunner.ts:162` comment names `pinsThatStillHold`; the function is `pinsFor`), 14 (stale comment in `e2e/hormuz.spec.ts` ~206–212 — delete it and assert the whole sentence), 15 (stale "Waiting on the engine fix" in `inspector.test.tsx` ~242), 16 (identity `.map` in `apiSource.ts` ~481), 17 (`DeltaRail.tsx` ~180 prints a raw ISO date where every other day goes through `toDay`), 18 (`spec/workbench/inspector.md` B2 and INV-workbench.54 speak of a `decomposition` field that does not exist — make the chapter say what the code does), 19 (`toSize(0)` prints a bare `0`).
(Findings 9–11 are the engine's and are going to the engine's owner.)

Re-run `npm run check` and `npx playwright test`; re-shoot the states the must-fixes touch (a wire's number before and after an edit; the same arrow on "as it was written"; H's tile after observing C; R selected). Report per item with the failing-then-passing test name, anything you disagree with, and the tails.

input.message:
Coordinator to F — your zero-strength analysis was right and I was wrong; it is pushed to #29. Kent has asked me to merge stack 04a, and an independent read-only reviewer went over #29 first. It found nothing that must be fixed in the engine, and confirmed the two rounding implementations agree on 300 095 inputs. Three should-fix findings are yours — same worktree and branch, commit, do not push:

9. **One rule, four copies**: "a version counts by its weights only for the claims the observation reaches" is spelled inline — `behind.weights if claim_id in behind.reweighted else numpy.ones_like(...)` — at `propagation.py` ~1490 and `diff.py` ~627, ~630, ~1068. Name it once (a small function beside `Versions`, e.g. `weights_for(behind, claim_id)`) and have `_counting_for`, the band's width and propagation read it. No behaviour change; pin that by comparing whole diffs before and after.
10. **`_counting_for`'s all-zero fallback is only right when BOTH worlds are empty.** The guard is on `minimum(in_a, in_b).sum() <= 0`, but `_band` falls back per world. If world A has survivors and world B has none, or their survivors are disjoint, the minimum is all zeros, the fallback counts every version equally, and the direction is read with weights NEITHER number was read with — the one sentence the amendment rests on, broken in a corner. Only reachable branch-against-branch. Decide the honest rule (mirror `_band`'s per-world fallback before taking the minimum? or say "no version counted in both numbers, so there is no direction to report" and return nothing?), state it once in the docstring and in `diff.md`, and test the one-sided and the disjoint case. Tell me which you chose and why.
11. **`_two_figures` turns a non-finite likelihood into `<.01` silently.** Reject, never repair: a NaN or infinity reaching the summary sentence should raise, not print a modest likelihood. (The browser twin does the same and is being told separately.)

input.message:
Coordinator to M — add this to your current round, at the top. The full measurement run (`make run-demo ONLY=hormuz CAP=15`, Sonnet 5, 26 minutes, paid) **crashed at the end and kept nothing**:

```
    3  accepted  The S&P Global Platts Japan-Korea Marker (JKM) front-month LNG…  (118s)
       so far: 4 calls, $0.73, 21 searches, 2,019 in / 26,749 out (19,710 of it thinking), 10m51s
  drafting the one intervention the card offers: '…but Iran is struck the next day'
    drafted
  File ".../engine/record.py", line 618, in <module>   raise SystemExit(main())
  File ".../engine/record.py", line 263, in run_one    update={"receipt": _with_the_insert(finished.receipt, its_calls)}
NameError: name '_with_the_insert' is not defined
```

**Root cause:** `record.py` has its `if __name__ == "__main__": raise SystemExit(main())` guard at line 618 and defines `_with_the_insert` at line 621 — BELOW the guard. Run as a program, `main()` executes before the rest of the module is defined. Imported by a test, everything is defined first, so every test passes and no static check sees it. And because the crash came before the write, `backend/.runs/` has nothing from this run — the second paid run whose receipt is lost, after the fix that was meant to make that impossible.

Fix it at the root, not the symptom:
1. The guard is the last thing in the file — in `record.py` and in every other module with one (`check_recordings.py`, anything else run with `-m`). Add a source-reading test, in the manner of `test_our_own_source.py`: in every module under `src/katalyst`, nothing but blank lines and comments follows the `__main__` guard.
2. **Test the program as a program.** At least one test runs `python -m katalyst.engine.record` (and `check_recordings`) as a subprocess against fake answers — add whatever seam that needs (for instance a setting naming a module whose factory returns the fake answerer, refused unless a test flag is set, or a `--fake` flag that only exists under tests; pick the simplest honest thing and say why) — through the WHOLE path: the generation, the scripted insert, the kept run, the verdict on the recording. It would have caught both this and the earlier `AttributeError` you found at line 601.
3. **"A paid run is never discarded" must survive a crash.** Keep the run incrementally or in a `finally`: the generation's transcript, receipt, map and events are written to `backend/.runs/` as soon as the generation ends and BEFORE the insert is drafted, then updated with the insert; an exception anywhere after the first paid call still leaves a file, with what was spent so far and the exception's one plain sentence in it. Test it with a fake answerer that raises on its Nth call, and with a crash injected after the generation.
4. One observation from this run for later, not for now: with the new prompt the hypothesis's three children were all `market` endings (Brent, TTF, JKM), so the frontier emptied and the map stopped at FOUR claims, depth one — the first-move-jumps-to-a-trade finding is worse, not better. Do not change the prompt in this round (the cassettes were just re-recorded); tell me in your report what you think is causing it and the smallest prompt change you would make, and I will batch it.
Then carry on with the four must-fix defects and the rest.

content.text:
The whole-map Sonnet 5 run failed at the last step, and nothing from it was kept.

**What happened.** The run lasted 26 minutes. The last visible state was 4 calls, $0.73, 21 searches, and 74% of written tokens spent on thinking. It then drafted the scripted "…but Iran is struck" insert and crashed with a `NameError` before writing anything to disk. I've booked it at $2, which puts the total at about $7.90 of $500.

**Why nothing caught it.** The recorder file has its "run me as a program" guard above a function the guard ends up calling. That only breaks when the file is actually run as a program. Every test imports the file, which defines everything first, so all 427 tests passed. Ruff and mypy can't see it either.

**The fix I've told M to make:**
- **The guard goes last in the file.** A test will enforce that for every module.
- **The recorder gets a subprocess test.** It runs as a real program, with fake answers, through the whole path including the insert.
- **A paid run is saved as it goes.** A crash at any point still leaves a file showing what was spent.
- **Handoff.** This is the second time a paid run lost its receipt, so I added it as lesson 16.

**Two things the partial output already shows:**
1. **Pace.** Four claims took about 11 minutes, which is around 2.7 minutes per tile with researched base rates. That matches the 200 seconds per call I measured while recording the cassettes.
2. **A new prompt problem.**
   - **What happened:** the claims are now properly standalone, for example "ICE Brent front-month futures settle at least 8% below…". But all three of the hypothesis's children came back as trades. The frontier emptied, and the map stopped at four claims, one step deep.
   - **What it means:** the rewritten prompt fixed the wording and made the jump-straight-to-a-trade problem worse.
   - **What's next:** I've asked M to diagnose it without touching the prompt, since the cassettes were only just re-recorded. It goes in the next batched round.

Still running: J on the join's must-fix items, and M on the recorder and the pipeline must-fix items. 04a merges as soon as J reports and I've verified it.

input.message:
Coordinator to J — round four verifies (227 tests) and your refusal on must-fix 3 was right: the browser cannot know which half of the engine's test failed; the engine will say so on the row in a later server pull request. One thing blocks the merge: **`e2e/hormuz.spec.ts` is flaky.** When I ran `npx playwright test` from cold, `the stored example, opened and edited by keyboard alone` failed 2 runs in 5 at line 177 — `opecBefore` was `""` — because it read a chip's `innerText()` once, straight away, before the engine's answer had arrived. I committed a fix on top of your branch (`83e6e6b`: wait with `toHaveText(/^\.\d+$/)` on R's and H's chips before reading). After it: 13 passes and **1 more failure in 14 runs, which I did not capture** — so there is at least one more read-before-ready somewhere in the three tests. Continuous integration is about 2.5× slower than this machine, so a one-in-fourteen flake here is a regular red build there.

Harden all three end-to-end tests at the root: every value the test reads must be WAITED FOR with a web-first assertion (`expect(locator).toHaveText/toContainText/toBeVisible`, or `expect.poll`) before it is read or compared — no bare `innerText()`/`textContent()` on anything that depends on the engine, on layout, on focus moving, or on an announcement; no fixed sleeps. Pay attention to: the numbers after each edit (a new world and a new diff are asked for — the old numbers are still on screen until they arrive, so "wait for a number" is not enough; wait for the thing that CHANGES, e.g. the status line's announcement for that edit, or the branch's name in the header, before reading), the wire's conditional after selection, the flip to "as it was written" and back, and the rail's rows. Then prove it: run `npx playwright test --repeat-each=40` (from cold at least once — stop any dev servers first so Playwright starts both halves itself) and paste the tail. Your fix addressed the symptom but not the cause, which is why it left one behind: **`toHaveText` reads `textContent`, and the failing read was `innerText`.** `innerText` is what the page *renders*, so it returns `""` for a tile React Flow has not measured yet — the wait was satisfied while the tile was still unrendered, and the very next line read `""` anyway.
